content_text: The Golden Globe Awards (in English, Golden Globe Awards) are presented every year to the best professionals in film and television, both inside and outside the United States. Presented since 1944 by the Hollywood Foreign Press Association (Hollywood Foreign Press Association), they are recognized as one of the highest honors a professional in these industries can receive, being the biggest critics' award, since the Oscar and the Emmy are awarded through evaluation by the respective peers.

The Golden Globes are presented at the beginning of each year (in the form of a dinner for nominees and guests), based on the votes of 93 members of the Hollywood Foreign Press Association, who are affiliated with media outlets outside the United States. Since 1961, the ceremony has been held at the Beverly Hilton Hotel in Los Angeles. Currently, the cable TV channel TNT holds the rights to broadcast the awards ceremony in Brazil. The Sony channel held the broadcast rights to the ceremony until 2006.

content_text: The first film industry awards presented by the Hollywood Foreign Correspondents Association (the forerunner of today's Hollywood Foreign Press Association) took place in early 1944 with an informal ceremony at 20th Century Fox. There, Jennifer Jones received the Best Actress award for The Song of Bernadette (1943), which also won Best Picture, while Paul Lukas took home the Best Actor laurels for Watch on the Rhine.

The awards were presented in the form of scrolls. The following year, the association's members held a contest to find a statuette design that best represented the organization's overall goals. Marina Cisternas, the group's president in 1945–46, came up with the idea of a shining globe on a cylindrical pedestal, to represent the world. Together with the presentation of the Golden Globe, the Hollywood Foreign Correspondents Association held its first gala social event in 1945 with a formal banquet at the Beverly Hills Hotel.
Going My Way (1944) won Best Picture, while Ingrid Bergman and Alexander Knox were named Best Actress and Best Actor for their performances in The Bells of St. Mary's (1945).

content_text: There were other important milestones in the history of the Golden Globes. In 1951, the association decided to split the nominees for best picture, actor and actress into two categories, drama and musical or comedy, so that no genre would be overlooked. In 1952, the HFPA created the Cecil B. DeMille Award to recognize "outstanding contributions to the world of entertainment." The first recipient of the award was DeMille himself.

Other unique awards that were discontinued over the years were the World Film Favorite, from 1951 to 1980, and the Newcomer Award, which went by several different names during its lifetime, from 1948 to 1983. Timothy Hutton, Bette Midler and Diana Ross were among the distinguished newcomers, while Steve McQueen, Doris Day and Barbra Streisand were some of the world film favorites.

In 1952, the Association created the Cecil B. DeMille Award to honor excellence in film. DeMille was the first to receive the award that bears his name. In 1956, the Golden Globes included some unique categories: the Trailblazer Award went to Walt Disney (American storytelling), Dinah Shore (American song), and Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz (American comedy). The latter paved the way for the inclusion of television categories alongside film, a tradition that continues to this day.

information.contentTitle: Sharon Tate & Roman Polanski at 1968 Golden Globe Awards

content_text: In 1957, five TV programs received Golden Globes: Cheyenne (best American Western); Mickey Mouse Club (best American children's program); Matinee Theatre (best American daytime drama); Playhouse 90 (best evening drama); This Is Your Life (best audience participation program).

Some categories, however, did not make it to today's Globes. From 1948 to 1963, the Globes recognized achievements in cinematography. Starting in 1951, separate cinematography Globes were awarded for black-and-white and color photography. The Longest Day (1962), High Noon (1952) and On the Waterfront (1954) received the former, while Quo Vadis (1951), Lawrence of Arabia (1962) and Brigadoon (1954) were among the winners in the color category.

In 2007, a new category was introduced: Best Animated Feature Film, with Pixar's Cars (2006) taking home the Globe. In 2018, the Carol Burnett Award was created to honor excellence in television; Carol Burnett herself was the recipient of the first award, in January 2019.

title: From 2021 to 2026
description:
In 2021, the Hollywood Foreign Press Association (HFPA), which had created and presented the Golden Globes since 1944, came under harsh criticism for the lack of diversity among its members (there was not a single Black journalist in the association) and for reports of payments and expensive gifts received by voters. Studios such as Netflix, Amazon and WarnerMedia cut ties with the association, and NBC refused to broadcast the 2022 ceremony, which ended up being a private event with no nominees, guests or press, and the winners announced on social media.

After a reform that expanded and diversified the voting body, the HFPA was dissolved on June 12, 2023: the Golden Globes brand and rights were bought by Dick Clark Productions (which has produced the show since 1993) and Eldridge Industries, and the association's philanthropic activities moved to the new Golden Globe Foundation. The 2023 edition was the last under the HFPA; since 2024 the award has been owned by Penske Media Eldridge, produced by Dick Clark Productions and voted on by an independent group of journalists from many countries (310 voters from 76 countries in the 2024 edition).

The new management also changed the categories: 2024 saw the debut of the Cinematic and Box Office Achievement award, which recognizes audience hits and has eight nominees (the first winner was Barbie), and in 2026 the awards began to include podcasts. The foreign film category is now officially called Best Motion Picture – Non-English Language.
